questions.answer: Reduced uncontrolled redundancy, improved data sharing and consistency, centralized security/integrity, concurrency control, backup/recovery and data independence.

questions.question: Differentiate logical and physical data independence.
questions.answer: Logical data independence permits changes to the conceptual schema without changing external views/programs. Physical data independence permits storage changes without changing the conceptual schema.

questions.question: Differentiate super key, candidate key and primary key.
questions.answer: A super key uniquely identifies tuples but may contain extra attributes. A candidate key is a minimal super key. One candidate key is selected as the primary key.

questions.question: Explain cardinality ratios in ER modelling.
questions.answer: Cardinality ratios specify how many entity instances may participate: one-to-one, one-to-many, many-to-one and many-to-many.

questions.question: Differentiate selection and projection.
questions.answer: Selection chooses tuples satisfying a predicate and is horizontal. Projection chooses specified attributes and is vertical, normally removing duplicate result tuples.

questions.question: What are entity integrity and referential integrity?
questions.answer: Entity integrity requires primary-key values to be unique and non-NULL. Referential integrity requires each non-NULL foreign-key value to match a referenced candidate/primary key.

questions.question: Differentiate DDL, DML, DCL and TCL with examples.
questions.answer: DDL defines structures: CREATE, ALTER, DROP. DML reads/changes data: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE. DCL controls privileges: GRANT, REVOKE. TCL controls transactions: COMMIT, ROLLBACK, SAVEPOINT.

questions.question: Differentiate WHERE and HAVING.
questions.answer: WHERE filters individual rows before grouping and cannot normally contain aggregate conditions. HAVING filters groups after GROUP BY and commonly uses aggregate expressions.

questions.question: What is a functional dependency?
questions.answer: X → Y means that whenever two tuples agree on attribute set X, they must also agree on Y. X is the determinant and Y is functionally dependent on X.

questions.question: Differentiate 3NF and BCNF.
questions.answer: 3NF permits X→A when X is a super key or A is prime. BCNF requires every non-trivial determinant X to be a super key, so BCNF is stricter.

questions.question: Explain the four ACID properties.
questions.answer: Atomicity: all or nothing. Consistency: rules remain satisfied. Isolation: concurrent transactions behave safely. Durability: committed changes survive failures.

questions.question: What is deadlock? Name two handling methods.
questions.answer: Deadlock is a cycle of transactions waiting indefinitely for one another's locks. It may be prevented using ordering/timeouts or detected with a wait-for graph and resolved by rolling back a victim.

questions.question: Explain the three-schema architecture and both kinds of data independence.
questions.answer: Describe external user views, the global conceptual schema and internal physical schema; external-conceptual and conceptual-internal mappings; logical and physical data independence with examples and benefits.

questions.question: Design and explain an ER model for a college database.
questions.answer: Include Student, Course, Teacher and Department entities; identifiers and attributes; enrolment and teaching relationships; appropriate cardinalities and participation constraints; resolve the many-to-many enrolment relationship when mapping to relations.

questions.question: Explain fundamental relational-algebra operations with examples.
questions.answer: Cover selection, projection, union, set difference, Cartesian product and rename; derive intersection and joins; explain division and express sample student-course queries.

questions.question: Explain SQL joins, aggregate queries, subqueries, views and indexes with syntax and examples.
questions.answer: Define inner/outer/cross/self joins; COUNT/SUM/AVG/MIN/MAX with GROUP BY and HAVING; scalar, multi-row and correlated subqueries; CREATE VIEW; CREATE INDEX; benefits and cautions.

questions.question: Normalize a relation from unnormalized form to Third Normal Form, explaining each step.
questions.answer: Identify repeating groups and atomic values for 1NF, candidate keys and partial dependencies for 2NF, then transitive dependencies for 3NF. Show decomposed schemas and verify lossless joins and preferably dependency preservation.

questions.question: Explain transaction states, serializability, locking, deadlocks and recovery.
questions.answer: Cover active, partially committed, committed, failed and aborted states; serial and concurrent schedules; conflict serializability; shared/exclusive locks and 2PL; deadlock handling; logs, checkpoints, undo and redo.

questions.question: Student rows have marks 80, 70, 70 and NULL. What does SELECT COUNT(marks), COUNT(*) FROM Student return?
questions.answer: 3 and 4. COUNT(marks) ignores NULL; COUNT(*) counts every row.

questions.question: Given Employee salaries 30000, 40000 and 50000, what is returned by SELECT AVG(salary) FROM Employee?
Department has D1 and D2. Employee contains only one employee in D1. How many rows does Department LEFT JOIN Employee produce?
questions.answer: Two rows: one matched row for D1 and one row for D2 with NULL Employee columns.

questions.question: What is the logical purpose of: SELECT dept_id FROM Employee GROUP BY dept_id HAVING COUNT(*) > 5?
questions.answer: It returns identifiers of departments having more than five employee rows.

questions.question: Relation R(A,B,C) has key (A,B) and dependency A→C. Which normal form is violated and why?
questions.answer: Second Normal Form is violated because non-prime attribute C depends on only part A of the composite key (A,B).

questions.question: T1 updates a balance and then rolls back. T2 read the uncommitted value. Name the anomaly.
questions.answer: Dirty read, also called uncommitted dependency. T2 observed a value that never became permanent.

questions.question: Convert an ER design with Student, Course and many-to-many Enrolment into relational schemas.
questions.answer:
STUDENT(StudentID PK, Name, ...)
COURSE(CourseID PK, Title, ...)
ENROLMENT(StudentID FK→STUDENT, CourseID FK→COURSE, EnrolDate, Grade, PRIMARY KEY(StudentID,CourseID)).

questions.question: Create a Student table with roll number, name, email, marks and department ID, using suitable constraints.
questions.answer:
CREATE TABLE Student(
 roll_no INT PRIMARY KEY,
 name VARCHAR(80) NOT NULL,
 email VARCHAR(120) UNIQUE,
 marks DECIMAL(5,2) CHECK(marks BETWEEN 0 AND 100),
 dept_id INT,
 FOREIGN KEY(dept_id) REFERENCES Department(dept_id)
);

questions.question: Write SQL to display each department name and its average salary, including departments with no employees.
questions.answer:
SELECT d.dept_name, AVG(e.salary) AS average_salary
FROM Department d
LEFT JOIN Employee e ON e.dept_id=d.dept_id
GROUP BY d.dept_id, d.dept_name;

questions.question: Write SQL to find employees earning more than the average salary of their own department.
Normalize ENROLMENT(StudentID, StudentName, CourseID, CourseName, TeacherID, TeacherName, Grade) to 3NF.
questions.answer:
Assume StudentID→StudentName, CourseID→CourseName,TeacherID, TeacherID→TeacherName, and (StudentID,CourseID)→Grade.
STUDENT(StudentID PK,StudentName)
TEACHER(TeacherID PK,TeacherName)
COURSE(CourseID PK,CourseName,TeacherID FK)
ENROLMENT(StudentID FK,CourseID FK,Grade,PRIMARY KEY(StudentID,CourseID)).
